<description>
{
 "summary": "Suppresses the response body when replying to HTTP HEAD requests while leaving the response headers (including Content-Length) unchanged. Per RFC 9110, HEAD responses must reflect the headers of an equivalent GET response without transmitting payload bytes. Accompanying functional tests verify raw socket behavior across RPC (405 error response) and REST (200 success response) endpoints.",
 "problem": "The HTTP server transmits body bytes in response to HEAD requests. Because RFC-compliant clients stop reading at the header terminator, the unconsumed body bytes remain in the connection buffer and are parsed as the beginning of the next HTTP response, desynchronizing pipelined or pooled keepalive connections behind reverse proxies like nginx.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description demonstrates that a raw HEAD request returns 'JSONRPC server handles only POST requests' body bytes after headers with a Content-Length header: 'A client that follows the specification stops reading after the header section, so the body bytes stay on the connection and are read as the start of the next response.'",
  "PR description notes exposure: 'Both the 405 reply of the RPC endpoint and the REST endpoints answer HEAD without authentication, so a client that is merely allowed to connect can trigger it.'"
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
